How does the heart move blood?
Follow blood through the heart, lungs and body tissues.
The right heart pumps to the lungs; the left heart pumps to the body.
Heart muscle contracts. Blood vessels carry blood to and from tissues.
Red blood cells carry much of the oxygen delivered to tissue.
Hemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in tissues.
The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs.
After gas exchange, blood returns to the left atrium through the pulmonary veins.
The left ventricle sends blood into the aorta. Smaller vessels deliver it to tissues.
After exchanging substances with tissues, blood returns through veins to the right atrium.
Blood pressure describes pressure in the arteries. It is not the same as blood flow or the amount the heart pumps in a minute.
Where does oxygen enter the blood?
Trace air and the two directions of gas exchange.
The lungs bring air close to the blood that flows through them.
Air and blood are separated by a thin barrier at the alveoli.
Red blood cells pick up oxygen in the lung capillaries.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide move in opposite directions across the barrier.
Air travels through the airways into the small air sacs of the lungs.
Oxygen crosses from the alveolar air into the surrounding capillaries.
At the same time, carbon dioxide moves from blood into the alveoli.
Air containing carbon dioxide leaves the lungs through the airways.
Ventilation moves air. Gas exchange transfers oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood. The two processes work together.
How do cells obtain usable energy?
Follow the transfer of energy from nutrients to ATP and cell work.
Organs receive nutrients through the circulation and use or store them in different ways.
Different tissues have different energy demands; muscle activity is one example.
Many cells use mitochondria to make much of their ATP when oxygen is available.
ATP can transfer usable energy to processes inside the cell.
Cells begin processing fuels such as glucose. Some of that processing happens outside mitochondria.
In the oxygen-using pathway, mitochondria help capture usable energy in ATP.
Cell processes such as moving substances across a membrane can use energy from ATP.
Metabolism includes both breaking down substances and building them. This diagram follows one energy-producing route, not every metabolic pathway.
How do nerve cells pass a signal?
Follow an electrical signal and a chemical message across a synapse.
The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves are parts of the nervous system.
Nervous tissue includes neurons and supporting glial cells.
A neuron can send an electrical signal along its axon.
At chemical synapses, neurotransmitters bind to receptors on a target cell.
An action potential travels down the axon toward its terminals.
At a chemical synapse, the arriving signal can trigger release of neurotransmitters.
Neurotransmitters cross the small gap and bind to receptors on the target cell.
An action potential and synaptic transmission are different stages. This example shows a chemical synapse, not every kind of connection.
How does food become absorbed nutrients?
Trace the route from chewing to absorption in the small intestine.
The mouth, stomach and intestines carry out different parts of digestion.
Smooth muscle helps move contents through the digestive tract.
Cells in the intestinal lining help take up digested nutrients.
Digestive enzymes help break large food molecules into smaller components.
Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces. After swallowing, the esophagus carries it to the stomach.
The stomach mixes food with digestive juices, then sends the mixture into the small intestine.
The small intestine absorbs many digested nutrients. They enter the blood or lymph, depending on the nutrient.
Digestion breaks food into smaller parts. Absorption is the later transfer of usable substances through the intestinal lining.
How do kidneys filter and recover fluid?
Follow filtration, selective reabsorption and the remaining fluid.
The kidneys filter blood and help regulate water and dissolved substances.
Nephrons contain a filtering structure and a tubular path for the filtrate.
Cells lining the tubules help control which substances move back toward the blood.
Water and small dissolved substances can enter the filtrate; some are reclaimed along the tubule.
Blood reaches the glomerulus, a cluster of small vessels in a nephron.
Water and small dissolved substances pass into the filtrate, while blood cells remain in the vessels.
The tubules return part of the water and useful substances to nearby blood vessels.
The remaining fluid and waste continue toward the urinary collecting system.
Kidney function depends on both filtration and what the tubules do afterward. A schematic cannot estimate an individual’s kidney function.
Oxygen enters the blood in the lungs. Much of it binds to hemoglobin inside red blood cells.
In tissues, some of the carried oxygen separates from hemoglobin and becomes available to cells.
This path describes binding and release qualitatively. It is not a molecular structure, oxygen saturation measurement, or chemical simulation.
